extraction_notes.note: The tagged displays (P), (G), (G'), (DG'), (G''), (DG''), (Q), (Q'), (DQ'), (BIL), (LIN) are numbered equation environments whose content is an optimization formulation; typed problem (Hard rule 4 promotion) rather than equation, confidence 0.9.

(P) is displayed twice with the same tag: the introduction states it over a generic class F, Section 2.2 over convex C^{1,1}_L functions. Treated as two problems (ProbP3 specializes ProbP1) instead of one repeated statement, since the function classes differ.
Numbered equations (2.1-style GM rate and Nesterov's FGM rate) retyped as external theorems: the text presents each as the known convergence rate of a cited method.

The appendix proof of Lemma 3.3 is split by subsections A.1 (S_0) and A.2 (S_1); emitted as two proof nodes, both proving LP3, with a uses edge from the second part to the first. The one-sentence section-A preamble is not in either node.

The feasibility remark for (BIL) cites the proof of Theorem 3.2 (T:gradLowBound), but the explicit dual feasible point is given in the proof of Theorem 3.1; the \ref edge from TP3 stays and a uses edge from PP3 was added.
Numerical bounds for HBM, FGM and the optimized method are given only as tables and a plot inside figures; the tables are not nodes, and the prose conclusions drawn from them are numerical claims.

The intermediate unnumbered relaxed PEP formulations in Section 3.1, the epsilon-optimality sentence (never used again), and the N=5 optimal-step algorithm shown in a figure were not extracted as nodes.
Algorithms are written as enumerate lists in \fbox rather than algorithm environments, so they are prose algorithm nodes; GM and FO have a single iteration line and get no steps.

nodes.name: First-order black-box optimization method
nodes.statement: According to this model, a \emph{first-order black-box} optimization method is an algorithm which has knowledge of the underlying space $\mathbb{R}^d$ and the family $\mathcal{F}$, the function itself is not known.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
differentia: has knowledge of the underlying space $\mathbb{R}^d$ and the family $\mathcal{F}$, the function itself is not known

nodes.name: First-order oracle
nodes.statement: To gain information on the function to be minimized, the algorithm queries a first order oracle, that is, a subroutine which given as input a point in $\mathbb{R}^d$, returns the value of the objective function and its gradient at that point.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
differentia: given as input a point in $\mathbb{R}^d$, returns the value of the objective function and its gradient at that point

nodes.name: First-order algorithm update rule
nodes.statement: The algorithm thus generates a finite sequence of points $\{x_i\in \mathbb{R}^d : i=0,\dots,N\}$, where at each step the algorithm can depend only on the previous steps, their function values and gradients via some rule $$ x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d,\; x_{i+1}={\cal A}(x_0,\dots,x_i; f(x_0),\dots,f(x_i); f'(x_0),\dots, f'(x_i)), \; i=0, \ldots, N-1, $$ where $f'(\cdot)$ stands for the gradient of $f(\cdot)$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: A first-order method generates $x_0,\dots,x_N$ where each $x_{i+1}$ depends only on previous points, their values and gradients.

nodes.name: Absolute inaccuracy
nodes.statement: Equivalently, we can measure the performance of an algorithm by looking at the absolute inaccuracy $$ \delta(f,x_N) = f(x_N) - f(x_\ast),$$ where $x_N$ is the result of the algorithm after making $N$ calls to the oracle.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Performance Estimation Problem (PEP)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \max \quad & f(x_N)-f(x_\ast) \\ \text{s.t. }\quad & f \in \mathcal{F},\\ & x_{i+1}={\cal A}(x_0,\dots,x_i; f(x_0),\dots,f(x_i); f'(x_0),\dots, f'(x_i)), \; i=0, \ldots, N-1,\\ & x_\ast \in X_\ast(f), \|x_\ast-x_0\|\leq R\\ & x_0, \ldots, x_N, x_\ast \in\mathbb{R}^d. \end{aligned} \tag{P}
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Worst-case absolute inaccuracy $f(x_N)-f(x_*)$ of a first-order method, maximized over all functions in $\mathcal{F}$ and admissible starting points.
nodes.label: P:baseproblemIntro

nodes.name: Gradient notation $f'(x)$
nodes.statement: For a differentiable function $f$, its gradient at $x$ is denoted by $f'(x)$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Symmetric matrices $\mathbb{S}^n$
nodes.statement: The set of symmetric matrices in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is denoted by $\mathbb{S}^n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Loewner order $A\succeq B$
nodes.statement: For two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$, $A\succeq B, (A \succ B)$ means $A-B \succeq 0 \,(A-B \succ 0)$ is positive semidefinite (positive definite).
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Canonical basis vectors $e_i$ and unit vector $\nu$
nodes.statement: We use $e_i$ for the $i$-th canonical basis vector in $\mathbb{R}^N$, which consists of all zero components, except for its $i$-th entry which is equal to one, and use $\nu$ to denote a unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Optimal value $\mathrm{val}(P)$
nodes.statement: For an optimization problem (P), $\mathrm{val}(P)$ stands for its optimal value.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Problem (M): unconstrained minimization over $\mathbb{R}^d$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a first-order algorithm for solving the optimization problem \begin{align*} \begin{aligned} (M)\quad \min\{ f(x):\, x \in \mathbb{R}^d\}. \end{aligned} \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions

nodes.name: Convex $C^{1,1}_L$ objective
nodes.statement: $f:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ is a convex function of the type $C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$, i.e., continuously differentiable with Lipschitz continuous gradient: \[ \|f'(x)-f'(y)\|\leq L \|x-y\|,\,\,\forall x,y\in \mathbb{R}^d, \] where $L>0$ is the Lipschitz constant.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is convex and continuously differentiable with $L$-Lipschitz gradient (class $C^{1,1}_L$).

nodes.name: Solvability of (M)
nodes.statement: We assume that (M) is solvable, i.e., the optimal set $X_*(f):=arg\,min f$ is nonempty, and for $x_*\in X_*(f)$ we set $f^*:=f(x_*).$
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions

nodes.name: Bounded initial distance $R$
nodes.statement: There exists $R>0$, such that the distance from $x_0$ to an optimal solution $x_\ast\in X_*(f)$ is bounded by $R$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions

nodes.name: Performance Estimation Problem (P) for convex $C^{1,1}_L$ functions
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \max \quad & f(x_N)-f(x_\ast) \\ \text{s.t. }\quad & f \in C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb{R}^d) \text{, $f$ is convex},\\ & x_{i+1}={\cal A}(x_0,\dots,x_i; f(x_0),\dots,f(x_i); f'(x_0),\dots, f'(x_i)), \; i=0, \ldots, N-1,\\ & x_\ast \in X_\ast(f), \|x_\ast-x_0\|\leq R,\\ & x_0, \ldots, x_N, x_\ast \in\mathbb{R}^d. \end{aligned} \tag{P}
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Idea and Main Approach
nodes.statement_short: The PEP (P) with the function class taken as convex functions in $C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$.
nodes.label: P:baseproblem

nodes.name: PEP relaxation approach
nodes.statement: An un-formal description of the underlying idea consists of two main steps as follows: \begin{itemize} \item Given an algorithm ${\cal A}$ that generates a finite sequence of points, to build a problem in finite dimension we replace the functional constraint $f\in C^{1,1}_L$ in \eqref{P:baseproblem} by new variables in $\mathbb{R}^d$. These variables, are the points $\{x_0, x_1, \ldots x_N, x_\ast \}$ themselves, the function values and their gradients at these points. Roughly speaking, this can be seen as a sort of discretization of $f$ at a selected set of points. \item To define constraints that relate the new variables, we use relevant/useful properties characterizing the family of convex functions in $C^{1,1}_L$, as well as the rule(s) describing the given algorithm ${\cal A}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Idea and Main Approach
nodes.statement_short: Turn the infinite-dimensional PEP into a finite one: replace $f$ by its values and gradients at the iterates, and constrain them by $C^{1,1}_L$ properties and the algorithm's rule.

nodes.name: Relaxations of (P) give valid upper bounds
nodes.statement: Note that any relaxation performed on the maximization problem \eqref{P:baseproblem} may increase its optimal value, however, the optimal value of the relaxed problem still remains a valid upper bound on $f(x_N)-f^\ast$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Idea and Main Approach
assumptions: any relaxation performed on the maximization problem \eqref{P:baseproblem}
conclusions: the optimal value of the relaxed problem still remains a valid upper bound on $f(x_N)-f^\ast$

nodes.name: Gradient Method (GM)
nodes.statement: Consider the gradient algorithm with constant step size, as applied to problem $(M)$, which generates a sequence of points as follows:\medskip \fbox{\parbox{14cm}{ {\bf Algorithm GM} \medskip \begin{enumerate} \setcounter{enumi}{-1} \item Input: $f\in C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ convex, $x_0\in \mathbb{R}^d.$ \item For $i=0,\dots,N-1$, compute $x_{i+1} = x_i - \frac{h}{L} f^\prime(x_i)$. \end{enumerate} }} \bigskip Here $h>0$ is fixed.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Gradient descent with constant step $h/L$: $x_{i+1}=x_i-\frac{h}{L}f'(x_i)$ for $N$ iterations.

nodes.name: Classical convergence rate of the gradient method
nodes.statement: f(x_N)-f^\ast \leq \frac{L\|x_0-x_\ast\|^2}{2N}, \quad \forall x_\ast \in X_\ast(f).
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
assumptions: for $h=1$
conclusions: f(x_N)-f^\ast \leq \frac{L\|x_0-x_\ast\|^2}{2N}, \quad \forall x_\ast \in X_\ast(f).
nodes.statement_short: For $h=1$ the gradient method satisfies $f(x_N)-f^*\le L\|x_0-x_*\|^2/(2N)$.
nodes.label: E:oldgradientbound

nodes.name: Co-coercivity inequality for convex $C^{1,1}_L$ functions
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex and $C^{1,1}_L$. Then, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2L} \|f^\prime(x)-f^\prime(y)\|^2 \leq f(x)-f(y)-\langle f^\prime(y), x-y\rangle, \;\mbox{for all} \; x,y\in \mathbb{R}^d. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
assumptions: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be convex and $C^{1,1}_L$.
conclusions: \frac{1}{2L} \|f^\prime(x)-f^\prime(y)\|^2 \leq f(x)-f(y)-\langle f^\prime(y), x-y\rangle, \;\mbox{for all} \; x,y\in \mathbb{R}^d.
nodes.label: prop:lip

nodes.name: Basic inequality for convex $C^{1,1}_L$ functions
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{2L} \|f^\prime(x)-f^\prime(y)\|^2 \leq f(x)-f(y)-\langle f^\prime(y), x-y\rangle, \;\mbox{for all} \; x,y\in \mathbb{R}^d.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
nodes.label: E:basicconvexprop

nodes.name: Starting point, GM iterates and minimizer $x_\ast$
nodes.statement: Let $x_0\in \mathbb{R}^d$ be any starting point, let $\{x_1,\dots,x_N \}$ be the points generated by Algorithm (GM) and let $x_\ast$ be a minimizer of $f$.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Interpolation constraints at the GM iterates
nodes.statement: & \frac{1}{2L} \|f^\prime(x_i)-f^\prime(x_j)\|^2 \leq f(x_i)-f(x_j)-\langle f^\prime(x_j), x_i-x_j\rangle, \quad i,j=0,\dots,N,\ast.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
nodes.label: E:basicconstraints

nodes.name: Normalized gaps $\delta_i$ and gradients $g_i$
nodes.statement: Now define \begin{align*} \delta_i &:= \frac{1}{L\|x_\ast-x_0\|^2}(f(x_i)-f(x_\ast)),\quad i=0,\dots,N, \ast \\ g_i &:= \frac{1}{L\|x_\ast-x_0\|}f^\prime(x_i),\quad i=0,\dots,N, \ast \end{align*} and note that we always have $\delta_\ast=0$ and $g_\ast=0$.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Normalize function gaps by $L\|x_*-x_0\|^2$ and gradients by $L\|x_*-x_0\|$.

nodes.name: Normalized interpolation constraints
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{2}\| g_i - g_j \| ^2 \leq \delta_i - \delta_j - \frac{\langle g_j, x_i-x_j \rangle}{\|x_\ast-x_0\|}, \quad i,j=0,\dots,N,\ast,
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
nodes.label: carf

nodes.name: Rotation invariance of the gradient PEP
nodes.statement: First, we observe that the problem is invariant under the transformation $g_i^\prime \leftarrow Q g_i$, $x_i^\prime \leftarrow Q x_i$ for any orthogonal transformation $Q$.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
conclusions: the problem is invariant under the transformation $g_i^\prime \leftarrow Q g_i$, $x_i^\prime \leftarrow Q x_i$ for any orthogonal transformation $Q$

nodes.name: Optimum of the PEP attained at $\|x_*-x_0\|=R$
nodes.statement: Finally, we note that the optimal solution for this problem is attained when $\|x_\ast-x_0\|=R$, and hence we can also eliminate the variables $x_0$ and $x_\ast$.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
conclusions: the optimal solution for this problem is attained when $\|x_\ast-x_0\|=R$

nodes.name: Gradient matrix $G$ and unit vectors $u_i$
nodes.statement: Let $G$ denote the $(N+1)\times d$ matrix whose rows are $g_0^T,\dots g_N^T$, and for notational convenience let $u_i\in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}$ denote the canonical unit vector \[ u_i = e_{i+1}, \quad i=0,\dots,N. \]
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Data matrices $A_{i,j}, B_{i,j}, C_i, D_i$ for GM
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} A_{i,j} &= \frac{1}{2} (u_i-u_j)(u_i-u_j)^T + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=i+1}^{j} h (u_j u_{t-1}^T+u_{t-1} u_j^T),\\ B_{i,j} &= \frac{1}{2} (u_i-u_j)(u_i-u_j)^T - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=j+1}^{i} h (u_j u_{t-1}^T+u_{t-1} u_j^T),\\ C_i &= \frac{1}{2} u_i u_i^T,\\ D_i &= \frac{1}{2} u_i u_i^T+ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{i} h (u_i u_{t-1}^T + u_{t-1} u_i^T), \end{aligned}
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
nodes.label: E:gradientmatrices

nodes.name: Gradient-method PEP (G) as a quadratic matrix program
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \max_{G\in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d},\delta \in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}}\ & LR^2 \delta_N \\ \text{s.t. } & \mathrm{tr} (G^T A_{i,j} G) \leq \delta_i - \delta_j,\quad i<j=0,\dots,N, \\ & \mathrm{tr}(G^T B_{i,j} G) \leq \delta_i - \delta_j,\quad j<i=0,\dots,N, \\ & \mathrm{tr}(G^T C_i G) \leq \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N, \\ & \mathrm{tr}(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G ) \leq - \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N. \end{aligned} \tag{G}
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Nonconvex quadratic matrix program in $(G,\delta)$ whose value bounds the worst case of GM.
nodes.label: P:gbound

nodes.name: (G) is a nonhomogeneous quadratic matrix program
nodes.statement: Problem (G) is a nonhomogeneous {\em Quadratic Matrix Program}, a class of problems recently introduced and studied by Beck \cite{beck-qm06}.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Relaxed gradient-method PEP (G')
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \max_{G\in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d},\delta \in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}}\ & LR^2 \delta_N \\ \text{s.t. } & \mathrm{tr} (G^T A_{i-1,i} G) \leq \delta_{i-1} - \delta_i,\quad i=1,\dots,N, \\ & \mathrm{tr}(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G ) \leq - \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N. \end{aligned} \tag{G$^\prime$}
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: (G) keeping only the constraints between consecutive iterates and those involving $x_*$.
nodes.label: P:gpr

nodes.name: Dimension reduction for quadratic matrix functions
nodes.statement: Let $f(X)=\mathrm{tr} (X^T Q X + 2 ba^T X)$ be a quadratic function, where $X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, $Q\in \mathbb{S}^n$, $a\in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $0\neq b\in \mathbb{R}^m$. Then \[ \inf_{X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}} f(X) = \inf_{\xi\in \mathbb{R}^n} f(\xi b^T). \]
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
assumptions: $f(X)=\mathrm{tr} (X^T Q X + 2 ba^T X)$ be a quadratic function, where $X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, $Q\in \mathbb{S}^n$, $a\in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $0\neq b\in \mathbb{R}^m$
conclusions: \inf_{X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}} f(X) = \inf_{\xi\in \mathbb{R}^n} f(\xi b^T).
nodes.statement_short: Minimizing $\mathrm{tr}(X^TQX+2ba^TX)$ over matrices reduces to minimizing over rank-one $X=\xi b^T$.
nodes.label: L:quadlemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.1
nodes.statement: First, we recall (this can be easily verified) that $\inf \{f(X): X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\} >-\infty$ if and only if $Q \succeq 0$, and there exists at least one solution ${\bar X}$ such that \begin{equation} Q{\bar X}+ ab^T=0 \; \Leftrightarrow\; {\bar X}^TQ +ba^T=0, \end{equation} i.e., the above is just $\nabla f (X)= 0$ and characterizes the minimizers of the convex function $f(X)$. Using (\ref{s1}) it follows that $\inf_X f(X)=f({\bar X})=\mathrm{tr} (ba^T{\bar X})$. Now, for any $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we have $f(\xi b^T)=\|b\|^2(\xi^TQ\xi + 2a^T\xi)$. Thus, likewise, $\inf\{f(\xi b^T): \xi \in \mathbb{R}^n\} >-\infty$ if and only if $Q \succeq 0$ and there exists ${\bar \xi}\in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that \begin{equation} Q{\bar \xi} + a=0,\end{equation} and using (\ref{s2}) it follows $\inf_\xi f(\xi b^T)=f({\bar \xi}b^T)=\|b\|^2a^T{\bar \xi}=\mathrm{tr} (ba^T{\bar \xi}b^T)$. Now, using (\ref{s1})-(\ref{s2}), one obtains ${\bar X}^TQ=-ba^T$ and $Q({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T)=0$, and hence it follows that \begin{eqnarray*} f({\bar X})-f({\bar \xi})&=&\mathrm{tr} (ba^T({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T))\\ &=&\mathrm{tr} (-{\bar X}^TQ({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T)=0. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Compare first-order optimality conditions of the matrix and rank-one problems and show the optimal values coincide.

nodes.statement: Q{\bar X}+ ab^T=0 \; \Leftrightarrow\; {\bar X}^TQ +ba^T=0,

nodes.label: s1

nodes.name: Lagrangian dual of (G')
nodes.statement: Consider problem \eqref{P:gpr} for any fixed $h\in \mathbb{R}$ and $L,R >0$. A Lagrangian dual of \eqref{P:gpr} is given by the following convex program: \begin{align*} \begin{aligned} \min_{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^N, t \in \mathbb{R}}\{\frac{1}{2} LR^2 t:\; \lambda \in \Lambda, \; S(\lambda, t) \succeq 0 \}, \end{aligned} \tag{DG$^\prime$} \end{align*} where $\Lambda:=\{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^N:\; \lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i \geq 0, \quad i=1,\dots,N-1,\; 1-\lambda_N \geq 0,\; \lambda_i \geq 0,\quad i=1,\dots,N\}$, the matrix $S(\cdot,\cdot)\in \mathbb{S}^{N+2}$ is given by \[ S(\lambda,t)=\begin{pmatrix} (1-h)S_0 + h S_1 & q \\ q^T & t \end{pmatrix}, \] with $q=(\lambda_1,\lambda_2-\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1},1-\lambda_N)^T$ and where the matrices $S_0, S_1\in \mathbb{S}^{N+1}$ are defined by: {\small \begin{equation} S_0= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & -\lambda_1 \\ -\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & -\lambda_2 \\ & -\lambda_2 & 2 \lambda_3 & -\lambda_3 \\ & & \ddots &\ddots & \ddots\\ & & & -\lambda_{N-1} & 2 \lambda_N & -\lambda_N \\ & & & & -\lambda_N & 1\\ \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} } and {\small {\begin{equation} S_1= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & \lambda_2-\lambda_1 &\dots &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} &1-\lambda_N \\ \lambda_2-\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} &1-\lambda_N \\ \vdots & & \ddots & &\vdots \\ \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} & \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} & & 2\lambda_N & 1-\lambda_N \\ 1-\lambda_N & 1-\lambda_N & \dots & 1-\lambda_N & 1 \\ \end{pmatrix} . \end{equation}}}
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
assumptions: Consider problem \eqref{P:gpr} for any fixed $h\in \mathbb{R}$ and $L,R >0$.
conclusions: A Lagrangian dual of \eqref{P:gpr} is given by the following convex program:
nodes.statement_short: (G') has a convex SDP dual in $(\lambda,t)$ with an $(N+2)\times(N+2)$ LMI built from $S_0$, $S_1$.
nodes.label: lem:dual

nodes.name: Dual problem (DG')
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \min_{\lambda \in \mathbb{R}^N, t \in \mathbb{R}}\{\frac{1}{2} LR^2 t:\; \lambda \in \Lambda, \; S(\lambda, t) \succeq 0 \}, \end{aligned} \tag{DG$^\prime$}
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: First note that both (G) and \eqref{P:gpr} are clearly feasible and $\mathrm{val} (G) \leq\mathrm{val}\eqref{P:gpr}$. Invoking Lemma \ref{lem:dual}, by weak duality for the pair of primal-dual problems \eqref{P:gpr} and \eqref{P:dualgpr}, we thus obtain that $\mathrm{val}\eqref{P:gpr}\leq \mathrm{val}\eqref{P:dualgpr}$ and hence: \begin{equation} f(x_N)-f^* \leq \mathrm{val} (G) \leq \mathrm{val} \eqref{P:gpr} \leq \mathrm{val} \eqref{P:dualgpr}. \end{equation} Now consider the following point $(\lambda,t)$ for the dual problem \eqref{P:dualgpr}: \begin{align*} \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i},\quad i=1,\dots,N, \\ t &= \frac{1}{2Nh+1}. \end{align*} Assuming that this point is \eqref{P:dualgpr}-feasible, it follows from (\ref{weak}) that $$ f(x_N)-f^* \leq \mathrm{val}\eqref{P:dualgpr} \leq \frac{L R^2}{4 N h+2}, $$ which proves the desired result. Thus, it remains to show that the above given choice $(\lambda, t)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:dualgpr}. First, it is easy to see that all the linear constraints of \eqref{P:dualgpr} on the variables $\lambda_i, i=1,\ldots ,N$ described through the set $\Lambda$ hold true. Now we prove that the matrix $S\equiv S(\lambda,t)$ is positive semidefinite. From Lemma~\ref{L:positivedefinitea0a1}, with $h \in [0,1]$, we get that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1$ is positive definite, as a convex combination of positive definite matrices. Next, we argue that the determinant of $S$ is zero. Indeed, take $u:=(1,\dots,1,-(2Nh+1))^T$, then from the definition of $S$ and the choice of $\lambda_i$ and $t$ it follows by elementary algebra that $Su=0$. To complete the argument, we note that the determinant of $S$ can also be found via the identity (see, e.g., \cite[Section~A.5.5]{boyd2004}): \[ \det(S) = (t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q) \det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1). \] Since we have just shown that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1 \succ 0$, then $\det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)>0$ and we get from the above identity that the value of $t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q$, which is the Schur complement of the matrix $S$, is equal to 0. By a well known lemma on the Schur complement \cite[Lemma~4.2.1]{ben2001lectures}, we conclude that $S$ is positive semidefinite.

nodes.name: Algorithm FGM' (FGM written in FO form)
nodes.statement: Observing that the gradient of the function is only evaluated on the {\em auxiliary sequence} of points $\{y_i\}$, we show in the next proposition that FGM fits in the scheme \text{FO}\xspace through the following algorithm: \fbox{\parbox{14cm}{ {\bf Algorithm \text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace} \medskip \begin{enumerate} \setcounter{enumi}{-1} \item Input: $f\in C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$, $x_0\in \mathbb{R}^d$, \item $y_1 \leftarrow x_0$, \item For $i=1,\dots,N-1$ compute: \begin{enumerate} \item$y_{i+1} \leftarrow y_i -\frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{i} h^{(i+1)}_{k} f^\prime(y_k)$, \end{enumerate} \item $x_N \leftarrow y_N -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N)$, \end{enumerate} }} with \begin{align} h^{(i+1)}_k = \begin{cases} \frac{t_{i}-1}{t_{i+1}}h^{(i)}_k & k+2\leq i, \\ \frac{t_{i}-1}{t_{i+1}}(h^{(i)}_{i-1}-1) & k = i-1, \\ 1+\frac{t_{i}-1}{t_{i+1}} & k = i \end{cases} \qquad (i=1,\dots,N-1, \ k=1,\dots,i). \end{align} and \begin{align*} t_i = \begin{cases} 1 & i=1 \\ \frac{1+\sqrt{1+4 t_{i-1}^2}}{2} & i>1. \end{cases} \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.1
nodes.statement: We will show by induction that the sequence $y_i$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace is identical to the sequence $y_i$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM}\xspace, and that the value of $x_N$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace is equal to the value of $x_N$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM}\xspace. First note that the sequence $t_i$ is defined by the two algorithms in the same way. Now let $\{x_i$, $y_i\}$ be the sequences generated by \text{FGM}\xspace and denote by $\{y_i^\prime\}$, $x_N^\prime$ the sequence generated by \text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace. Obviously, $y^\prime_1 = y_1$ and since $t_1=1$ we get using the relations \ref{E:nesterovsteps}: \begin{align*} y_2^\prime &= y_1^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(2)}_1 f^\prime(y_1^\prime) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} \left(1+\frac{t_{1}-1}{t_2} \right) f^\prime(y_1) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_1)= x_1 = y_2. \end{align*} Assuming $y_i^\prime = y_i$ for $i = 1,\dots,n$, we then have \begin{align*} y_{n+1}^\prime &= y_n^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_n f^\prime(y_n^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_{n-1} f^\prime(y_{n-1}^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} h^{(n+1)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\ &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} (1+\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}) f^\prime(y_n) - \frac{1}{L} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}(h^{(n)}_{n-1}-1) f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\ &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime)\right) \\ &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) +y_n^\prime-y_{n-1}^\prime\right) \\ &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} (x_n-x_{n-1}) \\ &= y_{n+1}. \end{align*} Finally, \[ x_N^\prime = y_N^\prime -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N^\prime) = y_N -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N) = x_N. \]
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples
nodes.statement_short: By induction on $n$, using the step-size recursion (4.3) to show $y'_{n+1}=y_{n+1}$; then $x'_N=x_N$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.1
nodes.statement: As (LIN) is a relaxation of \eqref{P:pblin}, it is enough to show that \eqref{P:pblin} can achieve the same objective value. Let $(r^\ast,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ be an optimal solution for (LIN). If $\lambda_i^\ast \neq 0$ for all $1\leq i \leq N$, then~\eqref{E:solvebil} satisfies all the equations in \eqref{E:definex} and therefore $(h,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:pblin}. Suppose $\lambda^\ast_m=0$ for some $1\leq m \leq N$ and that $m$ is the maximal index with this property. Then by the equality and non-negativity constraints in (LIN), we get that $\lambda^\ast_1=\lambda^\ast_2=\dots=\lambda^\ast_m=0$ and $\tau^\ast_0=\tau^\ast_1=\dots=\tau^\ast_{m-1}=0$. Let $S:=S(r,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast)$, then by the positive semidefinite constraint in (LIN), we have $S \succeq 0$. From the linear equalities connecting $\lambda$ and $\tau$ it follows that \[ S_{i,i}=\begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_1^\ast+\tau_0^\ast) = \lambda_1^\ast, &\quad i=1 \\ \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_i^\ast+\lambda_{i-1}^\ast+\tau_{i-1}^\ast) = \lambda_i^\ast, &\quad i=2,\dots,N \end{cases}, \] and we get that $S_{1,1}=\dots=S_{m,m}=0$. By the properties of positive semidefinite matrices we now get that $r_{i,k}^\ast=0$ for $i=1,\dots,m$ and $k=0,\dots,i-1$, hence the set of equations \eqref{E:definex} with the chosen values of $h_k^{(i)}$ is consistent.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3, part $S_0\succ0$
nodes.statement: We begin by showing that $S_0$ is positive definite. Recall that \[ S_0= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & -\lambda_1 \\ -\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & -\lambda_2 \\ & -\lambda_2 & 2 \lambda_3 & -\lambda_3 \\ & & \ddots &\ddots & \ddots\\ & & & -\lambda_{N-1} & 2 \lambda_N & -\lambda_N \\ & & & & -\lambda_N & 1\\ \end{pmatrix} \] for \begin{align*} \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i}, \qquad i=1,\dots,N. \end{align*} Let us look at $x^T S_0 x$ for any $x=(x_0,\dots,x_N)^T$: \begin{align*} x^T S_0 x &= \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} 2\lambda_{i+1} x_i^2 -2\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_{i+1} x_i x_{i+1} + x_N^2\\ &= \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_{i+1} (x_{i+1}-x_i)^2 +\lambda_1 x_0^2+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} (\lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i) x_i^2+(1-\lambda_N)x_N^2 \end{align*} which is always positive for $x\neq 0$. We conclude that $S_0$ is positive definite.
nodes.section: A.1 $S_0 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $x^TS_0x$ as a sum of squares with nonnegative coefficients from the monotone $\lambda_i$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3, part $S_1\succ0$
nodes.statement: We will show that $S_1$ is positive definite using Sylvester's criterion\footnote{Despite the interesting structure of the matrix $S_1$, this proof is quite involved. A simpler proof would be most welcome!}. Recall that \[ S_1= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & \lambda_2-\lambda_1 &\dots &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} &1-\lambda_N \\ \lambda_2-\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} &1-\lambda_N \\ \vdots & & \ddots & &\vdots \\ \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} & \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} & & 2\lambda_N & 1-\lambda_N \\ 1-\lambda_N & 1-\lambda_N & \dots & 1-\lambda_N & 1 \\ \end{pmatrix} \] for \begin{align*} \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i}, \qquad i=1,\dots,N. \end{align*} \paragraph{A recursive expression for the determinants} We begin by deriving a recursion rule for the determinant of matrices of the following form: \[ M_k= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & & \vdots\\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & d_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_k & a_k & a_k & \dots & a_k & d_k \end{pmatrix}. \] To find the determinant of $M_k$, subtract the one before last row multiplied by $\frac{a_{k}}{a_{k-1}}$ from the last row: the last row becomes \[ (0,\dots,0,a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1},d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}). \] Expanding the determinant along the last row we get \[ \det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1}-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det (M_k)_{k,k-1} \] where $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ denotes the $k,k-1$ minor: \[ (M_k)_{k,k-1}= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots \\ a_{k-2} & a_{k-2} & a_{k-2} & & d_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & a_{k-1} & a_k \end{pmatrix} . \] If we multiply the last column of $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ by $\frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}$ we get a matrix that is different from $M_{k-1}$ by only the corner element. Thus by basic determinant properties we get that \[ \frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}\det (M_k)_{k,k-1} = \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k-1}-d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}. \] Combining these two results, we have found the following recursion rule for $\det M_k$, $k\geq 2$: \begin{align*} &\det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1} \\&\qquad -(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1})\left(\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}} \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k}-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}\right) \\ &= \left((d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k})-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}\right) \det M_{k-1} -\left(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}\right)^2\det M_{k-2} \end{align*} or \begin{equation} \det M_k= \left(d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \right) \det M_{k-1}-a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \det M_{k-2} . \end{equation} Obviously, the recursion base cases are given by \begin{align*} & \det M_0 = d_0, \\ & \det M_1 = d_0 d_1-a_1^2. \end{align*} \paragraph{Closed form expressions for the determinants} Going back to our matrix, $S_1$, by choosing \begin{align*} & d_i = 2\frac{i+1}{2 N-i},\quad i=0,\dots,N-1 \\ & d_N = 1 \\ & a_i = \frac{i+1}{2 N-i}-\frac{i}{2 N+1-i},\quad i=1,\dots,N-1\\ & a_N = 1-\frac{N}{N+1} = \frac{1}{N+1}, \end{align*} we get that $M_k$ is the $k+1$'th leading principal minor of the matrix $S_1$. The recursion rule~\eqref{E:mrecursion} can now be solved for this choice of $a_i$ and $d_i$. The solution is given by: \begin{align} \det M_k =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-k)^2} \left( 1 +\sum_{i=0}^k \frac{2N-2k-1}{2N+4 N i - 2 i^2+1}\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2}, \end{align} for $k=0,\dots,N-1$, and \begin{align} \det M_N = \det L_1 =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2}\prod_{i=0}^{N-1} \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2} . \end{align} \paragraph{Verification} We now proceed to verify the expressions \eqref{E:mkdet} and \eqref{E:mndet} given above. We will show that these expressions satisfy the recursion rule \eqref{E:mrecursion} and the base cases of the problem. We begin by verifying the base cases: \begin{align*} \det M_0 & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N)^2}\left( 1 +\frac{2N-1}{2N+1}\right) \frac{1}{2N+1}= \frac{1}{N} = d_0, \end{align*} \begin{align*} \det M_1 & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-1)^2} \left( 1 +\frac{2N-3}{2N+1}+ \frac{2N-3}{6N -1}\right) \frac{1}{2N+1} \frac{6N-1}{(2N)^2} \\ &= \frac{28N^2-20N-1}{4N^2(2N-1)^2} = \frac{4}{N(2N-1)}-\left(\frac{2}{2N-1}-\frac{1}{2N}\right)^2= d_0 d_1-a_1^2. \end{align*} Now suppose $2 \leq k\leq N$. Denote \begin{align*} \alpha_k &= d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \\ &=\begin{cases} 4\frac{(2N+1)k-k^2-1}{(2N-k)^2}, &k<N\\ 3\frac{2N^2+2N-1}{(2N+1)^2}, &k=N \end{cases} \\ \beta_k &= a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \\ &=\begin{cases} \frac{(4 kN-2N-2k^2+4k-1)^2}{(2N-k)^2(2N-k+1)^2}, &k<N\\ \frac{(2N^2+2N-1)^2}{(N+1)^2(2N+1)^2}, &k=N \end{cases}, \end{align*} then the recursion rule \eqref{E:mrecursion} can be written as \begin{align*} & \det M_k= \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} - \beta_k \det M_{k-2}. \end{align*} Further denote \begin{align*} f_i &= \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-i)^2}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \\ g_i &= 2N-2i-1, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1,\\ x_i &= \frac{1}{2N+4 N i - 2 i^2+1}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \\ y_i &= \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \end{align*} then the solution \eqref{E:mkdet} becomes \begin{align*} \det M_k =& f_k \left(1+g_k \sum_{i=0}^{k} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} y_i, \end{align*} and \eqref{E:mndet} becomes \begin{align*} \det M_N =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2} \prod_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i. \end{align*} Substituting \eqref{E:mkdet} in the RHS of \eqref{E:mrecursion} we get that for $k=2,\dots,N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} - \beta_k \det M_{k-2}\\ &= \alpha_k f_{k-1} \left(1+g_{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i - \beta_k f_{k-2}\left(1+g_{k-2}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i \right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-2} y_i\\ &= \left( \alpha_k f_{k-1} \left(1+g_{k-1} x_{k-1}+g_{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right)-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i \right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i\\ &= \left( \alpha_k f_{k-1}(1+ g_{k-1} x_{k-1}) -\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2}+\left( \alpha_k f_{k-1} g_{k-1}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2}\right) \sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i. \end{align*} It is straightforward (although somewhat involved) to verify that for $k<N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_k f_{k-1} (1+ g_{k-1} x_{k-1}) -\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} = f_k y_k (1+g_k x_{k-1}+g_k x_k), \end{align*} and \begin{align*} & \alpha_k f_{k-1}g_{k-1}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2} = f_k g_k y_k. \end{align*} We therefore get \begin{align*} & \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} -\beta_k \det M_{k-2} \\ & = \left( f_k y_k(1+g_k x_{k-1}+g_k x_k)+ f_k g_k y_k \sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i\\ & = f_k \left( 1+g_k \sum_{i=0}^{k} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} y_i\\ & = \det M_k, \end{align*} and thus \eqref{E:mkdet} satisfies \eqref{E:mrecursion}. It is also possible to show that \begin{align*} & \alpha_N f_{N-1}(1+ g_{N-1} x_{N-1}) -\frac{\beta_N}{y_{N-1}} f_{N-2} = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2}, \\ & \alpha_N f_{N-1} g_{N-1}-\frac{\beta_N}{y_{N-1}} f_{N-2} g_{N-2} = 0, \end{align*} thus, for $k=N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_N \det M_{N-1} -\beta_N \det M_{N-2} \\ & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2} \prod_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i \\ & = \det M_N, \end{align*} and the expression \eqref{E:mndet} is also verified. To complete the proof, note that the closed form expressions for $\det M_k$ consist of sums and products of positive values, hence $\det M_k$ is positive, and thus follows from Sylvester's criterion that $S_1$ is positive definite.
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Sylvester's criterion: derive a three-term recursion for the leading principal minors, guess closed forms and verify them. The closed forms are sums and products of positive terms.

nodes.name: Discretize f
nodes.statement: Given an algorithm ${\cal A}$ that generates a finite sequence of points, to build a problem in finite dimension we replace the functional constraint $f\in C^{1,1}_L$ in \eqref{P:baseproblem} by new variables in $\mathbb{R}^d$. These variables, are the points $\{x_0, x_1, \ldots x_N, x_\ast \}$ themselves, the function values and their gradients at these points. Roughly speaking, this can be seen as a sort of discretization of $f$ at a selected set of points.
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Idea and Main Approach
nodes.statement_short: Replace $f$ by new variables: the iterates, function values and gradients there.

nodes.name: Add constraints
nodes.statement: To define constraints that relate the new variables, we use relevant/useful properties characterizing the family of convex functions in $C^{1,1}_L$, as well as the rule(s) describing the given algorithm ${\cal A}$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Basic Idea and Main Approach
nodes.statement_short: Relate the variables by $C^{1,1}_L$ convexity properties and the algorithm's rule.

nodes.statement: $x_1 \leftarrow x_0 - \frac{\alpha}{L} f^\prime(x_0)$

nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples
nodes.statement_short: Gradient step plus momentum term $\beta(x_i-x_{i-1})$.

nodes.name: Optimality of the matrix problem
nodes.statement: First, we recall (this can be easily verified) that $\inf \{f(X): X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\} >-\infty$ if and only if $Q \succeq 0$, and there exists at least one solution ${\bar X}$ such that \begin{equation} Q{\bar X}+ ab^T=0 \; \Leftrightarrow\; {\bar X}^TQ +ba^T=0, \end{equation} i.e., the above is just $\nabla f (X)= 0$ and characterizes the minimizers of the convex function $f(X)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Recall: bounded below iff $Q\succeq0$, minimizers solve $Q\bar X+ab^T=0$.

nodes.name: Value at the matrix minimizer
nodes.statement: Using (\ref{s1}) it follows that $\inf_X f(X)=f({\bar X})=\mathrm{tr} (ba^T{\bar X})$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Infimum equals $\mathrm{tr}(ba^T\bar X)$.

nodes.name: Rank-one problem
nodes.statement: Now, for any $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we have $f(\xi b^T)=\|b\|^2(\xi^TQ\xi + 2a^T\xi)$. Thus, likewise, $\inf\{f(\xi b^T): \xi \in \mathbb{R}^n\} >-\infty$ if and only if $Q \succeq 0$ and there exists ${\bar \xi}\in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that \begin{equation} Q{\bar \xi} + a=0,\end{equation} and using (\ref{s2}) it follows $\inf_\xi f(\xi b^T)=f({\bar \xi}b^T)=\|b\|^2a^T{\bar \xi}=\mathrm{tr} (ba^T{\bar \xi}b^T)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Same analysis for $X=\xi b^T$, minimizer solves $Q\bar\xi+a=0$.

nodes.name: Values coincide
nodes.statement: Now, using (\ref{s1})-(\ref{s2}), one obtains ${\bar X}^TQ=-ba^T$ and $Q({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T)=0$, and hence it follows that \begin{eqnarray*} f({\bar X})-f({\bar \xi})&=&\mathrm{tr} (ba^T({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T))\\ &=&\mathrm{tr} (-{\bar X}^TQ({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T)=0. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Combine both optimality conditions to show the two infima are equal.

nodes.name: Recast as minimization
nodes.statement: For convenience, we recast \eqref{P:gpr} as a minimization problem, and we also omit the fixed term $LR^2$ from the objective. That is, we consider the equivalent problem \eqref{P:agpr} defined by \begin{align*} \begin{aligned} \min_{G\in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d},\delta \in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}}\ & -\delta_N \\ \text{s.t. } & \mathrm{tr} (G^T A_{i-1,i} G) \leq \delta_{i-1} - \delta_i,\quad i=1,\dots,N, \\ & \mathrm{tr}(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G ) \leq - \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N. \end{aligned} \tag{G$^{\prime\prime}$} \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite (G') as the minimization (G'').

nodes.name: Lagrangian
nodes.statement: Attaching the dual multipliers $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N) \in \mathbb{R}^N_{+}$ and $\tau:=(\tau_0, \ldots ,\tau_N)^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}_{+}$ to the first and second set of inequalities respectively, and using the notation $\delta=(\delta_0, \ldots ,\delta_N)$, we get that the Lagrangian of this problem is given as a sum of two separable functions in the variables $(\delta, G)$: \begin{eqnarray*} L(G,\delta, \lambda, \tau)&=& -\delta_N+\sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i(\delta_i - \delta_{i-1}) + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i \delta_i \\ & &+ \sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i \mathrm{tr}(G^T A_{i-1,i} G)+ \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i \left( \mathrm{tr}(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G) \right)\\ & \equiv & L_1(\delta, \lambda, \tau)+ L_2(G,\lambda, \tau). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Attach multipliers $\lambda,\tau$; the Lagrangian separates in $\delta$ and $G$.

nodes.name: Dual problem
nodes.statement: The dual objective function is then defined by $$H(\lambda, \tau)=\min_{G, \delta} L(G,\delta, \lambda\, \tau)=\min_\delta L_1(\delta, \lambda, \tau)+ \min_{G} L_2(G, \lambda, \tau),$$ and the dual problem of \eqref{P:agpr} is then given by \begin{align*} \begin{aligned} \max \{ H(\lambda, \tau):\; \lambda \in\mathbb{R}^{N}_{+}, \tau \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}_{+}\}. \end{aligned} \tag{DG$^{\prime\prime}$} \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Define the dual objective $H$ and dual problem (DG'').

nodes.name: Minimize over $\delta$
nodes.statement: Since $L_1(\cdot,\lambda, \tau)$ is linear in $\delta$, we have $\min_\delta L_1(\delta,\lambda, \tau) =0$ whenever \begin{eqnarray} -\lambda_1 +\tau_0 &= & 0, \nonumber\\ \lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}+\tau_i &=& 0\quad (i=1,\dots,N-1), \\ -1+\lambda_N+\tau_N &=& 0, \nonumber \end{eqnarray} and $-\infty$ otherwise.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Linear in $\delta$: finite only under relations (eqtau).

nodes.name: Reduce $G$ to rank one
nodes.statement: Invoking Lemma~\ref{L:quadlemma}, we get \begin{align*} \min_{G\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d}} L_2(G,\lambda, \tau) = \min_{w\in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}} L_2(w \nu^T,\lambda, \tau). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 3.1 to restrict $G=w\nu^T$.

nodes.name: LMI form
nodes.statement: Therefore for any $(\lambda,\tau)$ satisfying (\ref{eqtau}), we have obtained that the dual objective reduces to \begin{eqnarray*} H(\lambda, \tau) &=& \min_{w \in \mathbb{R}^{N+1}}\{w^T \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i A_{i-1,i} + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i D_i \right) w + \tau^T w \}\\ &=& \max_{t\in \mathbb{R}} \{-\frac{1}{2}t : w^T \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i A_{i-1,i} + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i D_i \right) w + \tau^T w \leq -\frac{1}{2}t,\ \forall w\in \mathbb{R}^{N+1} \}\\ &=& \max_{t\in \mathbb{R}} \left\{ -\frac{1}{2}t: \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i A_{i-1,i} + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i D_i & \frac{1}{2} \tau \\ \frac{1}{2}\tau^T & \frac{1}{2}t \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0 \right\}. \end{eqnarray*} where the last equality follows from the well known lemma \cite[Page~163]{ben2001lectures}\footnote{Let $M$ be a symmetric matrix. Then, $x^TMx + 2 b^Tx+ c \geq 0, \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ if and only if the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} M & b\\ b^T & c \end{pmatrix}$ is positive semidefinite.}.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Express the dual objective via a PSD block-matrix condition.

nodes.name: Compute the matrix sums
nodes.statement: Now, recalling the definition of the matrices $A_{i-1,i}, D_i$ (see (\ref{E:gradientmatrices})), we obtain {\small \[ \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i A_{i-1,i} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & (h-1)\lambda_1 \\ (h-1)\lambda_1 & \lambda_1+\lambda_2 & (h-1)\lambda_2 \\ & (h-1)\lambda_2 & \lambda_2 +\lambda_3 & (h-1)\lambda_3 \\ & & \ddots &\ddots & \ddots\\ & & & (h-1)\lambda_{N-1} & \lambda_{N-1}+ \lambda_N & (h-1)\lambda_N \\ & & & & (h-1)\lambda_N & \lambda_N\\ \end{pmatrix} \] } and {\small \[ \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i D_i = \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} \tau_0 & h\tau_1 & \dots &h\tau_{N-1} &h\tau_N \\ h\tau_1 & \tau_1 & &h\tau_{N-1} &h\tau_N \\ \vdots & & \ddots & &\vdots \\ h\tau_{N-1} & h\tau_{N-1} & & \tau_{N-1} & h\tau_N \\ h\tau_N & h\tau_N & \dots & h\tau_N & \tau_N \\ \end{pmatrix}. \] }
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Explicit forms of $\sum\lambda_iA_{i-1,i}$ and $\sum\tau_iD_i$.

nodes.name: Eliminate $\tau$
nodes.statement: Finally, using the relations (\ref{eqtau}) to eliminate $\tau_i$, and recalling that $\mathrm{val}\!\eqref{P:agpr}$ was defined as $-LR^2 \mathrm{val}\!\eqref{P:gpr}$, the desired form of the stated dual problem follows.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Use (eqtau) to eliminate $\tau$ and obtain (DG').

nodes.name: Relaxation ordering
nodes.statement: First note that both (G) and \eqref{P:gpr} are clearly feasible and $\mathrm{val} (G) \leq\mathrm{val}\eqref{P:gpr}$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Weak duality
nodes.statement: Invoking Lemma \ref{lem:dual}, by weak duality for the pair of primal-dual problems \eqref{P:gpr} and \eqref{P:dualgpr}, we thus obtain that $\mathrm{val}\eqref{P:gpr}\leq \mathrm{val}\eqref{P:dualgpr}$ and hence: \begin{equation} f(x_N)-f^* \leq \mathrm{val} (G) \leq \mathrm{val} \eqref{P:gpr} \leq \mathrm{val} \eqref{P:dualgpr}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Dual candidate

nodes.name: Reduce to feasibility
nodes.statement: Thus, it remains to show that the above given choice $(\lambda, t)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:dualgpr}.

nodes.name: Linear constraints

nodes.name: PSD constraint
nodes.statement: Now we prove that the matrix $S\equiv S(\lambda,t)$ is positive semidefinite. From Lemma~\ref{L:positivedefinitea0a1}, with $h \in [0,1]$, we get that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1$ is positive definite, as a convex combination of positive definite matrices. Next, we argue that the determinant of $S$ is zero. Indeed, take $u:=(1,\dots,1,-(2Nh+1))^T$, then from the definition of $S$ and the choice of $\lambda_i$ and $t$ it follows by elementary algebra that $Su=0$. To complete the argument, we note that the determinant of $S$ can also be found via the identity (see, e.g., \cite[Section~A.5.5]{boyd2004}): \[ \det(S) = (t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q) \det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1). \] Since we have just shown that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1 \succ 0$, then $\det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)>0$ and we get from the above identity that the value of $t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q$, which is the Schur complement of the matrix $S$, is equal to 0. By a well known lemma on the Schur complement \cite[Lemma~4.2.1]{ben2001lectures}, we conclude that $S$ is positive semidefinite.

nodes.statement_short: Show $S(\lambda,t)\succeq0$.

nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Schur-complement determinant formula.

nodes.name: Conclude PSD
nodes.statement: By a well known lemma on the Schur complement \cite[Lemma~4.2.1]{ben2001lectures}, we conclude that $S$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
nodes.statement_short: Schur complement lemma gives $S\succeq0$.

nodes.name: Induction plan
nodes.statement: We will show by induction that the sequence $y_i$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace is identical to the sequence $y_i$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM}\xspace, and that the value of $x_N$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace is equal to the value of $x_N$ generated by Algorithm~\text{FGM}\xspace.
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples
nodes.statement_short: Show by induction that the $y$ sequences coincide.

nodes.name: Same $t_i$
nodes.statement: First note that the sequence $t_i$ is defined by the two algorithms in the same way.
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples
nodes.statement_short: Both algorithms define $t_i$ identically.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: Now let $\{x_i$, $y_i\}$ be the sequences generated by \text{FGM}\xspace and denote by $\{y_i^\prime\}$, $x_N^\prime$ the sequence generated by \text{FGM$^\prime$}\xspace. Obviously, $y^\prime_1 = y_1$ and since $t_1=1$ we get using the relations \ref{E:nesterovsteps}: \begin{align*} y_2^\prime &= y_1^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(2)}_1 f^\prime(y_1^\prime) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} \left(1+\frac{t_{1}-1}{t_2} \right) f^\prime(y_1) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_1)= x_1 = y_2. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Assuming $y_i^\prime = y_i$ for $i = 1,\dots,n$, we then have \begin{align*} y_{n+1}^\prime &= y_n^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_n f^\prime(y_n^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_{n-1} f^\prime(y_{n-1}^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} h^{(n+1)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\ &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} (1+\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}) f^\prime(y_n) - \frac{1}{L} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}(h^{(n)}_{n-1}-1) f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\ &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime)\right) \\ &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) +y_n^\prime-y_{n-1}^\prime\right) \\ &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} (x_n-x_{n-1}) \\ &= y_{n+1}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples
nodes.statement_short: Expand $y'_{n+1}$ with the step-size recursion to obtain $y_{n+1}$.

nodes.name: Final point
nodes.statement: Finally, \[ x_N^\prime = y_N^\prime -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N^\prime) = y_N -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N) = x_N. \]

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: As (LIN) is a relaxation of \eqref{P:pblin}, it is enough to show that \eqref{P:pblin} can achieve the same objective value.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: Since (LIN) relaxes (BIL), suffices that (BIL) attains the same value.

nodes.name: Case all $\lambda_i^*\ne0$
nodes.statement: Let $(r^\ast,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ be an optimal solution for (LIN). If $\lambda_i^\ast \neq 0$ for all $1\leq i \leq N$, then~\eqref{E:solvebil} satisfies all the equations in \eqref{E:definex} and therefore $(h,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:pblin}.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: The recursive rule solves (E:definex) exactly.

nodes.name: Case some $\lambda_m^*=0$
nodes.statement: Suppose $\lambda^\ast_m=0$ for some $1\leq m \leq N$ and that $m$ is the maximal index with this property. Then by the equality and non-negativity constraints in (LIN), we get that $\lambda^\ast_1=\lambda^\ast_2=\dots=\lambda^\ast_m=0$ and $\tau^\ast_0=\tau^\ast_1=\dots=\tau^\ast_{m-1}=0$. Let $S:=S(r,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast)$, then by the positive semidefinite constraint in (LIN), we have $S \succeq 0$. From the linear equalities connecting $\lambda$ and $\tau$ it follows that \[ S_{i,i}=\begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_1^\ast+\tau_0^\ast) = \lambda_1^\ast, &\quad i=1 \\ \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_i^\ast+\lambda_{i-1}^\ast+\tau_{i-1}^\ast) = \lambda_i^\ast, &\quad i=2,\dots,N \end{cases}, \] and we get that $S_{1,1}=\dots=S_{m,m}=0$. By the properties of positive semidefinite matrices we now get that $r_{i,k}^\ast=0$ for $i=1,\dots,m$ and $k=0,\dots,i-1$, hence the set of equations \eqref{E:definex} with the chosen values of $h_k^{(i)}$ is consistent.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: Zero multipliers force the corresponding $r^*_{i,k}=0$.

nodes.name: Maximal zero index
nodes.statement: Suppose $\lambda^\ast_m=0$ for some $1\leq m \leq N$ and that $m$ is the maximal index with this property. Then by the equality and non-negativity constraints in (LIN), we get that $\lambda^\ast_1=\lambda^\ast_2=\dots=\lambda^\ast_m=0$ and $\tau^\ast_0=\tau^\ast_1=\dots=\tau^\ast_{m-1}=0$.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: Earlier $\lambda^*$ and $\tau^*$ also vanish.

nodes.name: Zero diagonal of PSD matrix
nodes.statement: Let $S:=S(r,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast)$, then by the positive semidefinite constraint in (LIN), we have $S \succeq 0$. From the linear equalities connecting $\lambda$ and $\tau$ it follows that \[ S_{i,i}=\begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_1^\ast+\tau_0^\ast) = \lambda_1^\ast, &\quad i=1 \\ \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_i^\ast+\lambda_{i-1}^\ast+\tau_{i-1}^\ast) = \lambda_i^\ast, &\quad i=2,\dots,N \end{cases}, \] and we get that $S_{1,1}=\dots=S_{m,m}=0$.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: $S\succeq0$ from (LIN) and its diagonal entries $S_{i,i}=\lambda_i^*$ vanish for $i\le m$.

nodes.name: Consistency
nodes.statement: By the properties of positive semidefinite matrices we now get that $r_{i,k}^\ast=0$ for $i=1,\dots,m$ and $k=0,\dots,i-1$, hence the set of equations \eqref{E:definex} with the chosen values of $h_k^{(i)}$ is consistent.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class \text{FO}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: PSD with zero diagonal forces zero rows, so $r^*_{i,k}=0$ and the equations are consistent.

nodes.name: Recall $S_0$
nodes.statement: We begin by showing that $S_0$ is positive definite. Recall that \[ S_0= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & -\lambda_1 \\ -\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & -\lambda_2 \\ & -\lambda_2 & 2 \lambda_3 & -\lambda_3 \\ & & \ddots &\ddots & \ddots\\ & & & -\lambda_{N-1} & 2 \lambda_N & -\lambda_N \\ & & & & -\lambda_N & 1\\ \end{pmatrix} \] for \begin{align*} \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i}, \qquad i=1,\dots,N. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.1 $S_0 \succ 0$

nodes.name: Sum of squares
nodes.statement: Let us look at $x^T S_0 x$ for any $x=(x_0,\dots,x_N)^T$: \begin{align*} x^T S_0 x &= \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} 2\lambda_{i+1} x_i^2 -2\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_{i+1} x_i x_{i+1} + x_N^2\\ &= \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_{i+1} (x_{i+1}-x_i)^2 +\lambda_1 x_0^2+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} (\lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i) x_i^2+(1-\lambda_N)x_N^2 \end{align*} which is always positive for $x\neq 0$.
nodes.section: A.1 $S_0 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Write $x^TS_0x$ as a nonnegative combination of squares, positive for $x\ne0$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We conclude that $S_0$ is positive definite.
nodes.section: A.1 $S_0 \succ 0$

nodes.name: Plan via Sylvester
nodes.statement: We will show that $S_1$ is positive definite using Sylvester's criterion\footnote{Despite the interesting structure of the matrix $S_1$, this proof is quite involved. A simpler proof would be most welcome!}. Recall that \[ S_1= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & \lambda_2-\lambda_1 &\dots &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} &1-\lambda_N \\ \lambda_2-\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} &1-\lambda_N \\ \vdots & & \ddots & &\vdots \\ \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} & \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} & & 2\lambda_N & 1-\lambda_N \\ 1-\lambda_N & 1-\lambda_N & \dots & 1-\lambda_N & 1 \\ \end{pmatrix} \] for \begin{align*} \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i}, \qquad i=1,\dots,N. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Use Sylvester's criterion on $S_1$.

nodes.name: Determinant recursion
nodes.statement: \paragraph{A recursive expression for the determinants} We begin by deriving a recursion rule for the determinant of matrices of the following form: \[ M_k= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & & \vdots\\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & d_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_k & a_k & a_k & \dots & a_k & d_k \end{pmatrix}. \] To find the determinant of $M_k$, subtract the one before last row multiplied by $\frac{a_{k}}{a_{k-1}}$ from the last row: the last row becomes \[ (0,\dots,0,a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1},d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}). \] Expanding the determinant along the last row we get \[ \det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1}-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det (M_k)_{k,k-1} \] where $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ denotes the $k,k-1$ minor: \[ (M_k)_{k,k-1}= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots \\ a_{k-2} & a_{k-2} & a_{k-2} & & d_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & a_{k-1} & a_k \end{pmatrix} . \] If we multiply the last column of $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ by $\frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}$ we get a matrix that is different from $M_{k-1}$ by only the corner element. Thus by basic determinant properties we get that \[ \frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}\det (M_k)_{k,k-1} = \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k-1}-d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}. \] Combining these two results, we have found the following recursion rule for $\det M_k$, $k\geq 2$: \begin{align*} &\det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1} \\&\qquad -(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1})\left(\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}} \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k}-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}\right) \\ &= \left((d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k})-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}\right) \det M_{k-1} -\left(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}\right)^2\det M_{k-2} \end{align*} or \begin{equation} \det M_k= \left(d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \right) \det M_{k-1}-a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \det M_{k-2} . \end{equation} Obviously, the recursion base cases are given by \begin{align*} & \det M_0 = d_0, \\ & \det M_1 = d_0 d_1-a_1^2. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Three-term recursion for determinants of matrices $M_k$ of the given form.

nodes.name: Closed forms
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Closed form expressions for the determinants} Going back to our matrix, $S_1$, by choosing \begin{align*} & d_i = 2\frac{i+1}{2 N-i},\quad i=0,\dots,N-1 \\ & d_N = 1 \\ & a_i = \frac{i+1}{2 N-i}-\frac{i}{2 N+1-i},\quad i=1,\dots,N-1\\ & a_N = 1-\frac{N}{N+1} = \frac{1}{N+1}, \end{align*} we get that $M_k$ is the $k+1$'th leading principal minor of the matrix $S_1$. The recursion rule~\eqref{E:mrecursion} can now be solved for this choice of $a_i$ and $d_i$. The solution is given by: \begin{align} \det M_k =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-k)^2} \left( 1 +\sum_{i=0}^k \frac{2N-2k-1}{2N+4 N i - 2 i^2+1}\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2}, \end{align} for $k=0,\dots,N-1$, and \begin{align} \det M_N = \det L_1 =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2}\prod_{i=0}^{N-1} \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2} . \end{align}
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Specialize to $S_1$ and state closed forms for its leading minors.

nodes.name: Verification
nodes.statement: \paragraph{Verification} We now proceed to verify the expressions \eqref{E:mkdet} and \eqref{E:mndet} given above. We will show that these expressions satisfy the recursion rule \eqref{E:mrecursion} and the base cases of the problem. We begin by verifying the base cases: \begin{align*} \det M_0 & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N)^2}\left( 1 +\frac{2N-1}{2N+1}\right) \frac{1}{2N+1}= \frac{1}{N} = d_0, \end{align*} \begin{align*} \det M_1 & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-1)^2} \left( 1 +\frac{2N-3}{2N+1}+ \frac{2N-3}{6N -1}\right) \frac{1}{2N+1} \frac{6N-1}{(2N)^2} \\ &= \frac{28N^2-20N-1}{4N^2(2N-1)^2} = \frac{4}{N(2N-1)}-\left(\frac{2}{2N-1}-\frac{1}{2N}\right)^2= d_0 d_1-a_1^2. \end{align*} Now suppose $2 \leq k\leq N$. Denote \begin{align*} \alpha_k &= d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \\ &=\begin{cases} 4\frac{(2N+1)k-k^2-1}{(2N-k)^2}, &k<N\\ 3\frac{2N^2+2N-1}{(2N+1)^2}, &k=N \end{cases} \\ \beta_k &= a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \\ &=\begin{cases} \frac{(4 kN-2N-2k^2+4k-1)^2}{(2N-k)^2(2N-k+1)^2}, &k<N\\ \frac{(2N^2+2N-1)^2}{(N+1)^2(2N+1)^2}, &k=N \end{cases}, \end{align*} then the recursion rule \eqref{E:mrecursion} can be written as \begin{align*} & \det M_k= \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} - \beta_k \det M_{k-2}. \end{align*} Further denote \begin{align*} f_i &= \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-i)^2}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \\ g_i &= 2N-2i-1, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1,\\ x_i &= \frac{1}{2N+4 N i - 2 i^2+1}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \\ y_i &= \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \end{align*} then the solution \eqref{E:mkdet} becomes \begin{align*} \det M_k =& f_k \left(1+g_k \sum_{i=0}^{k} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} y_i, \end{align*} and \eqref{E:mndet} becomes \begin{align*} \det M_N =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2} \prod_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i. \end{align*} Substituting \eqref{E:mkdet} in the RHS of \eqref{E:mrecursion} we get that for $k=2,\dots,N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} - \beta_k \det M_{k-2}\\ &= \alpha_k f_{k-1} \left(1+g_{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i - \beta_k f_{k-2}\left(1+g_{k-2}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i \right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-2} y_i\\ &= \left( \alpha_k f_{k-1} \left(1+g_{k-1} x_{k-1}+g_{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right)-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i \right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i\\ &= \left( \alpha_k f_{k-1}(1+ g_{k-1} x_{k-1}) -\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2}+\left( \alpha_k f_{k-1} g_{k-1}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2}\right) \sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i. \end{align*} It is straightforward (although somewhat involved) to verify that for $k<N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_k f_{k-1} (1+ g_{k-1} x_{k-1}) -\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} = f_k y_k (1+g_k x_{k-1}+g_k x_k), \end{align*} and \begin{align*} & \alpha_k f_{k-1}g_{k-1}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2} = f_k g_k y_k. \end{align*} We therefore get \begin{align*} & \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} -\beta_k \det M_{k-2} \\ & = \left( f_k y_k(1+g_k x_{k-1}+g_k x_k)+ f_k g_k y_k \sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i\\ & = f_k \left( 1+g_k \sum_{i=0}^{k} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} y_i\\ & = \det M_k, \end{align*} and thus \eqref{E:mkdet} satisfies \eqref{E:mrecursion}. It is also possible to show that \begin{align*} & \alpha_N f_{N-1}(1+ g_{N-1} x_{N-1}) -\frac{\beta_N}{y_{N-1}} f_{N-2} = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2}, \\ & \alpha_N f_{N-1} g_{N-1}-\frac{\beta_N}{y_{N-1}} f_{N-2} g_{N-2} = 0, \end{align*} thus, for $k=N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_N \det M_{N-1} -\beta_N \det M_{N-2} \\ & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2} \prod_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i \\ & = \det M_N, \end{align*} and the expression \eqref{E:mndet} is also verified.
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Check the closed forms satisfy the recursion and base cases.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: To complete the proof, note that the closed form expressions for $\det M_k$ consist of sums and products of positive values, hence $\det M_k$ is positive, and thus follows from Sylvester's criterion that $S_1$ is positive definite.
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: All leading minors are positive, so $S_1\succ0$.

nodes.name: Define $M_k$
nodes.statement: We begin by deriving a recursion rule for the determinant of matrices of the following form: \[ M_k= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & & \vdots\\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & d_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_k & a_k & a_k & \dots & a_k & d_k \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$

nodes.name: Row operation
nodes.statement: To find the determinant of $M_k$, subtract the one before last row multiplied by $\frac{a_{k}}{a_{k-1}}$ from the last row: the last row becomes \[ (0,\dots,0,a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1},d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}). \]
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$

nodes.name: Expand along last row
nodes.statement: Expanding the determinant along the last row we get \[ \det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1}-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det (M_k)_{k,k-1} \] where $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ denotes the $k,k-1$ minor: \[ (M_k)_{k,k-1}= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots \\ a_{k-2} & a_{k-2} & a_{k-2} & & d_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & a_{k-1} & a_k \end{pmatrix} . \]
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$

nodes.name: Minor relation
nodes.statement: If we multiply the last column of $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ by $\frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}$ we get a matrix that is different from $M_{k-1}$ by only the corner element. Thus by basic determinant properties we get that \[ \frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}\det (M_k)_{k,k-1} = \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k-1}-d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}. \]
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$

nodes.name: Recursion
nodes.statement: Combining these two results, we have found the following recursion rule for $\det M_k$, $k\geq 2$: \begin{align*} &\det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1} \\&\qquad -(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1})\left(\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}} \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k}-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}\right) \\ &= \left((d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k})-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}\right) \det M_{k-1} -\left(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}\right)^2\det M_{k-2} \end{align*} or \begin{equation} \det M_k= \left(d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \right) \det M_{k-1}-a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \det M_{k-2} . \end{equation}
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Combine to get the recursion (A.1).

nodes.name: Base cases
nodes.statement: Obviously, the recursion base cases are given by \begin{align*} & \det M_0 = d_0, \\ & \det M_1 = d_0 d_1-a_1^2. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$

nodes.name: Specialize to $S_1$
nodes.statement: Going back to our matrix, $S_1$, by choosing \begin{align*} & d_i = 2\frac{i+1}{2 N-i},\quad i=0,\dots,N-1 \\ & d_N = 1 \\ & a_i = \frac{i+1}{2 N-i}-\frac{i}{2 N+1-i},\quad i=1,\dots,N-1\\ & a_N = 1-\frac{N}{N+1} = \frac{1}{N+1}, \end{align*} we get that $M_k$ is the $k+1$'th leading principal minor of the matrix $S_1$.
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Choose $d_i, a_i$ so $M_k$ is a leading minor of $S_1$.

nodes.name: Closed-form solution
nodes.statement: The recursion rule~\eqref{E:mrecursion} can now be solved for this choice of $a_i$ and $d_i$. The solution is given by: \begin{align} \det M_k =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-k)^2} \left( 1 +\sum_{i=0}^k \frac{2N-2k-1}{2N+4 N i - 2 i^2+1}\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2}, \end{align} for $k=0,\dots,N-1$, and \begin{align} \det M_N = \det L_1 =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2}\prod_{i=0}^{N-1} \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2} . \end{align}
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$

nodes.name: Base cases
nodes.statement: We now proceed to verify the expressions \eqref{E:mkdet} and \eqref{E:mndet} given above. We will show that these expressions satisfy the recursion rule \eqref{E:mrecursion} and the base cases of the problem. We begin by verifying the base cases: \begin{align*} \det M_0 & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N)^2}\left( 1 +\frac{2N-1}{2N+1}\right) \frac{1}{2N+1}= \frac{1}{N} = d_0, \end{align*} \begin{align*} \det M_1 & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-1)^2} \left( 1 +\frac{2N-3}{2N+1}+ \frac{2N-3}{6N -1}\right) \frac{1}{2N+1} \frac{6N-1}{(2N)^2} \\ &= \frac{28N^2-20N-1}{4N^2(2N-1)^2} = \frac{4}{N(2N-1)}-\left(\frac{2}{2N-1}-\frac{1}{2N}\right)^2= d_0 d_1-a_1^2. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Verify $k=0,1$.

nodes.name: Recursion coefficients
nodes.statement: Now suppose $2 \leq k\leq N$. Denote \begin{align*} \alpha_k &= d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \\ &=\begin{cases} 4\frac{(2N+1)k-k^2-1}{(2N-k)^2}, &k<N\\ 3\frac{2N^2+2N-1}{(2N+1)^2}, &k=N \end{cases} \\ \beta_k &= a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \\ &=\begin{cases} \frac{(4 kN-2N-2k^2+4k-1)^2}{(2N-k)^2(2N-k+1)^2}, &k<N\\ \frac{(2N^2+2N-1)^2}{(N+1)^2(2N+1)^2}, &k=N \end{cases}, \end{align*} then the recursion rule \eqref{E:mrecursion} can be written as \begin{align*} & \det M_k= \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} - \beta_k \det M_{k-2}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Name the coefficients $\alpha_k,\beta_k$.

nodes.name: Shorthand
nodes.statement: Further denote \begin{align*} f_i &= \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-i)^2}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \\ g_i &= 2N-2i-1, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1,\\ x_i &= \frac{1}{2N+4 N i - 2 i^2+1}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \\ y_i &= \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \end{align*} then the solution \eqref{E:mkdet} becomes \begin{align*} \det M_k =& f_k \left(1+g_k \sum_{i=0}^{k} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} y_i, \end{align*} and \eqref{E:mndet} becomes \begin{align*} \det M_N =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2} \prod_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $f_i,g_i,x_i,y_i$.

nodes.name: Substitute
nodes.statement: Substituting \eqref{E:mkdet} in the RHS of \eqref{E:mrecursion} we get that for $k=2,\dots,N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} - \beta_k \det M_{k-2}\\ &= \alpha_k f_{k-1} \left(1+g_{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i - \beta_k f_{k-2}\left(1+g_{k-2}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i \right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-2} y_i\\ &= \left( \alpha_k f_{k-1} \left(1+g_{k-1} x_{k-1}+g_{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right)-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i \right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i\\ &= \left( \alpha_k f_{k-1}(1+ g_{k-1} x_{k-1}) -\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2}+\left( \alpha_k f_{k-1} g_{k-1}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2}\right) \sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$

nodes.name: Case $k<N$
nodes.statement: It is straightforward (although somewhat involved) to verify that for $k<N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_k f_{k-1} (1+ g_{k-1} x_{k-1}) -\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} = f_k y_k (1+g_k x_{k-1}+g_k x_k), \end{align*} and \begin{align*} & \alpha_k f_{k-1}g_{k-1}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2} = f_k g_k y_k. \end{align*} We therefore get \begin{align*} & \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} -\beta_k \det M_{k-2} \\ & = \left( f_k y_k(1+g_k x_{k-1}+g_k x_k)+ f_k g_k y_k \sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i\\ & = f_k \left( 1+g_k \sum_{i=0}^{k} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} y_i\\ & = \det M_k, \end{align*} and thus \eqref{E:mkdet} satisfies \eqref{E:mrecursion}.
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
nodes.statement_short: Two identities verify the recursion for $k<N$.

nodes.name: Case $k=N$
nodes.statement: It is also possible to show that \begin{align*} & \alpha_N f_{N-1}(1+ g_{N-1} x_{N-1}) -\frac{\beta_N}{y_{N-1}} f_{N-2} = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2}, \\ & \alpha_N f_{N-1} g_{N-1}-\frac{\beta_N}{y_{N-1}} f_{N-2} g_{N-2} = 0, \end{align*} thus, for $k=N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_N \det M_{N-1} -\beta_N \det M_{N-2} \\ & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2} \prod_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i \\ & = \det M_N, \end{align*} and the expression \eqref{E:mndet} is also verified.
nodes.section: A.2 $S_1 \succ 0$
